back: f is continuous at x = a when f(a) is defined, the limit lim_{x→a} f(x) exists, and the two are equal.
Continuous from the right at a if lim_{x→a⁺} f(x) = f(a); from the left if lim_{x→a⁻} f(x) = f(a).
If f is continuous on [a, b], then every value between f(a) and f(b) is attained somewhere in [a, b].
Every differentiable function is continuous. The converse is false: |x| is continuous but not differentiable at 0.
For y = u(x)^{v(x)} or a product, take ln y, differentiate implicitly: y'/y = (u'/u)v + v' ln u.
d/dx [e^{f(x)}] = e^{f(x)} f'(x). d/dx [ln f(x)] = f'(x)/f(x).
If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), then ∃ c ∈ (a,b) with f'(c) = [f(b)−f(a)]/(b−a).
If f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b), then ∃ c with f'(c)=0.
For f,g both continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), ∃ c with (f(b)−f(a))g'(c) = (g(b)−g(a))f'(c).
